items.title: Isolated Linux workstations for autonomous AI agents
items.story_key: story|title:isolated linux workstations for autonomous ai agents
items.content_excerpt: Give your AI coding agents their own machines — not your credentials. Isolated Linux workstations with full autonomy, on Linux and macOS. Give your AI coding agents their own machines, not your credentials. isx.run is the website, with the full documentation. An AI agent in your terminal can read your API keys, your GitHub token, your ~/.ssh and every repo you have checked out. Your IDE and build tools execute anything the agent writes. Each agent works in its own machine and asks for no approval, so you can run many side by side and build automations that run with nobody watching. isx runs on Linux and macOS, on your hardware, and your repositories and credentials stay there. Agents are the main use, not the only one. The same disposable machines are ideal for triaging untrusted patches, reproducing bug reports and testing on a clean system. Built with Quarkus and Tamboui , powered by Incus system containers. Written in Java, compiled to native binaries with GraalVM . isx was formerly known as incus-spawn. Requires Linux, or macOS 15 (Sequoia) or later ( Installation ); isx init sets up the rest, or your coding agent can do it all for you . On a fresh Linux host, isx init adds you to the incus-admin group and finishes its run in that group. Other terminals get the group at your next login, or in each one with newgrp incus-admin . A template is a machine image you build once: an OS, tools and repos. The template below adds Claude Code to the built-in tpl-minimal template. Save it as ~/.config/incus-spawn/images/tpl-agent.yaml , or run isx templates new tpl-agent and paste it over the skeleton that opens in your editor: Claude Code signs in with the Claude credential you set up in isx init ; isx account add claude adds one later. Claude Code never sees the credential: the proxy adds the credential to each request after the request leaves the instance. If you did not install the services isx init offers, start them before building: isx proxy start on Linux, isx vm start && isx proxy start on macOS. For another agent, replace claude with codex , pi , opencode , gemini-cli , antigravity , bob or copilot ; see Agents . Pi and opencode use your Claude credential too, unless their provider names another API ( Pi , opencode ). To give the agent a project, add repos: ( Declarative Repos ). items.title: Keeping AI Coding Agent Memory Relevant as Code Changes
items.story_key: story|title:keeping ai coding agent memory relevant as code changes
items.content_excerpt: How Enola uses source code analysis and symbol tracking to help coding agents retrieve earlier investigations and verify them against evolving codebases. Coding agents can retain information between sessions. They can save investigations, remember architectural decisions, and retrieve knowledge that would otherwise disappear when a session ends. Imagine an agent investigating a bug in a pointer-movement handler. It identifies the relevant implementation and records its conclusions. A month later, another agent investigates a related problem and retrieves those notes. The function may have moved, been renamed, or changed substantially. Even adding lines elsewhere in the file can make an old line reference point to unrelated code. There is another problem: the next agent might never retrieve the investigation because it describes the same code using different terminology. Or it might retrieve an investigation of an unrelated function with the same name. We wanted to understand how often these problems occur in real repositories, how well coding agents handle them, and whether connecting persistent knowledge to source-code structure could improve retrieval and reuse. An agent can preserve knowledge in a Markdown file, a session summary, or a dedicated memory system such as Cognee . These approaches make earlier investigations available to future sessions. Memory systems can also organize and retrieve knowledge based on the task an agent is performing. The pointer-move handler contains the crop-move logic. Check this function when investigating crop dragging. A file path and line number provide a starting point, but line numbers describe positions in a particular version of a file, not durable references to functions. Function names are more useful, but they are not necessarily unique and can change. A Git commit makes the original source recoverable, although the agent still needs to connect that historical implementation to the current code. These limitations also affect retrieval. A memory system relying on textual or semantic similarity might miss earlier investigations that use different descriptions of the same function, or retrieve observations about unrelated implementations with similar names. Enola builds a structural representation of a codebase by extracting symbols and their relationships from source code. Its locate functionality resolves a source location to a symbol: The result includes the symbol's identifier, name, and body_hash , a fingerpri

items.title: Leaky AI supply chain is exposing secret user data at an alarming rate
items.story_key: story|title:leaky ai supply chain is exposing secret user data at an alarming rate
items.content_excerpt: Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn’t stay private. Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of AWS access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible. “We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday . “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.” Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one

items.title: Combatting adversarial distillation
items.summary: OpenAI’s layered approach to adversarial distillation combines model training, safeguards, detection, and enforcement to protect against capability extraction.
items.story_key: story|title:combatting adversarial distillation
items.content_excerpt: How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry. As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly important role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked. We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry. Our approach to adversarial distillation combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity. We place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model. W e’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming , we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards. Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why . items.title: Inkling 2 Mini on vLLM: Day-0 Support for a Looped Model
items.summary: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini from day 0: a looped MoE that runs its middle layers three times, with per-pass KV caches, gated messages between passes, fused kernels and DSpark speculative decoding.
items.story_key: model:vllm|variant:mini|title:inkling 2 mini on vllm day 0 support for a looped model
items.content_excerpt: Thinking Machines announced Inkling 2 Mini today. vLLM supports it and its variable-loop research checkpoint, TML-d24-varloop-research , on day 0 on NVIDIA Blackwell, Hopper and DGX Spark. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped model: its middle 12 layers run three times per token with shared weights, each pass with its own KV cache and gated messages from the pass before. It is a multimodal MoE with 26B total and 3.5B active parameters, up to 1M tokens of context and a native DSpark speculator. We provide a Docker image with Inkling 2 Mini support, vllm/vllm-openai:inkling-2-mini . You can serve the model with: And the variable-loop research checkpoint, here with 2 passes and one KV cache shared across passes: Figure 1. The prelude and coda run once; the loop core runs three passes, each reading messages from the one before. Prelude, core, coda. The 24 layers split into a prelude (layers 0–5), a loop core (layers 6–17) and a coda (layers 18–23). The prelude and coda run once each; the core runs three passes with shared weights, and the coda continues from the last pass. Each group of six layers is one block of the block attention residuals used in Inkling 2 Small, so one pass of the core produces exactly two blocks. Every pass starts from the prelude's output. A plain looped model feeds pass p's output into pass p + 1. Here, all three passes start from that same output, and pass p + 1 sees pass p only through messages. Messages are read at every sublayer. From the second pass on, each core sublayer input (the attention's query, key and value inputs and the MLP input) gets its own message, read from the previous pass's two blocks by an attention-residual read with a learned query per layer and input type. A rank-64 controller then merges the message into the input, per channel: With 12 core layers and 4 inputs each, every later pass reads 48 messages per token. Because the query, key and value inputs get different messages, the sliding-window layers, which project all three from one input in the first pass, take three separate inputs in later passes. Each pass keeps its own memory. Every core layer has a KV cache and a conv-state cache per pass, so pass p attends to the keys and values that pass p computed for earlier tokens. The model has 24 layers but 48 KV caches and 48 conv-state caches. DSpark draft from inside the loop. items.story_key: story|variant:mini|title:welcome inkling 2 mini cutting edge performance for your local setup
items.content_excerpt: TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost. Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release! We ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware. This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup. Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones. Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384. The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights. Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages . Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). items.title: Ultimate guide for fixing your team’s API keys
items.summary:
Most Gemini prototypes start the same way. You grab an API key from Google AI Studio, then paste it into your coding agent to start building a prototype. That speed is the point, and shouldn’t be slowed down. 

The trouble starts later, when the prototype gets real users and the key comes along unchanged. By then it usually isn't one key. Every developer has their own, often several, sitting in .env files, shell profiles and chat threads. The app has one more, baked into its config.

For example, imagine an account that normally spends $180 a month. One of those keys ends up in a public repo, a Slack channel or a mobile app bundle. Automated scrapers find it within minutes and use it to run large workloads. By the time the first billing alert arrives, the bill is in the tens of thousands. Under the shared responsibility model, the customer pays for usage made with their own valid credentials. For a seed-stage company, that’s runway gone in a weekend.

In our recent post, 10 questions every startup should answer before moving to production with their AI prototype, we covered the whole path from prototype to production. This post goes deeper on one part of it: getting off raw API keys entirely.

Here is what this guide covers:

  • Authorize your people. Give everyone on the team one login with Application Default Credentials and use it to call Gemini, Claude and open models. Steps 1 and 2 take about five minutes.

  • Authorize your application. Run your app under its own service account with only the access it needs. Steps 3 and 4.

  • Lock down what's left. Move the remaining keys into Secret Manager, then add spend caps, guardrails and monitoring. Step 5 and the closing sections.

The code for every step is in a companion repo with runnable samples and offline tests.

Why a raw key is different

An AI Studio key is a bearer token. Whoever holds it can use it. It doesn't expire on its own. It isn't tied to a machine, a person or a workload. It has no spending limit unless you add one. When someone leaves the company, nobody knows which keys to revoke.

That is fine on your laptop while you are the only user. It stops being fine when any of these is true:

  • A key has left your laptop. It was shared in chat, committed to a repo or deployed to a server.

  • More than one person on the team needs to call the API.

  • You are spending more than a few hundred dollars a month, or you are about to onboard paying customers.

If one of those describes you, do the switch this week.

Before changing anything, find out where your keys are. The repo includes a small scanner that looks for strings shaped like Google API keys and for api_key= set to a literal value. It reports the file and line but never the key itself. It also exits with an error, so you can drop it into CI:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'python -m step1_keyless_auth.scan_for_keys .'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f7711b07fd0>)])]>

Step one: Give each person one login

Each person on the team runs one command:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud auth application-default login'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f771128c210>)])]>

A browser window opens, you sign in with your work account and gcloud stores a short-lived credential on your machine. Every Google Cloud SDK finds it automatically. There is no key to copy, paste or leak.

Then point your tools at the team project:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=my-startup-dev'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f771128cd90>)])]>

Someone has to grant you access to the project first. Step four shows how.

Step two: Call any model with that login

That single credential works for every model in Model Garden, not only Gemini. You don't need new accounts, new keys or separate invoices. Within each SDK, switching models means changing one string.

Gemini, with the Google Gen AI SDK. If your prototype builds the client with api_key=..., this is the only change:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'from google import genai\r\n\r\nclient = genai.Client(enterprise=True, project="my-startup-dev", location="global")\r\nresp = client.models.generate_content(model="gemini-4-hydrogen", contents="Hi")\r\nprint(resp.text)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f771128ce10>)])]>

enterprise=True sends the call to Gemini Platform instead of AI Studio. Older samples call the same flag vertexai=True, and current SDK versions accept both.

Claude, with Anthropic's SDK and the same login:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'from anthropic import AnthropicVertex\r\n\r\nclient = AnthropicVertex(project_id="my-startup-dev", region="global")\r\nmsg = client.messages.create(\r\n model="claude-sonnet-5-5",\r\n max_tokens=512,\r\n messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}],\r\n)\r\nprint(msg.content[0].text)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f771128ca50>)])]>

Open models such as OpenAI's gpt-oss, with the OpenAI SDK pointed at Google Cloud:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'import google.auth, google.auth.transport.requests\r\nfrom openai import OpenAI\r\n\r\ncreds, _ = google.auth.default(scopes=["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"])\r\ncreds.refresh(google.auth.transport.requests.Request())\r\n\r\nclient = OpenAI(\r\n base_url="https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/my-startup-dev/locations/global/endpoints/openapi",\r\n api_key=creds.token, # a one-hour token from your login, not a stored key\r\n)\r\nresp = client.chat.completions.create(\r\n model="openai/gpt-oss-120b-maas",\r\n messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}],\r\n)\r\nprint(resp.choices[0].message.content)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f771128de90>)])]>

Two things to know:

  • Partner models like Claude need a one-time Enable on their Model Garden card in each project. After that, everyone with access can call them.

  • OpenAI's GPT-6 models arrived in Model Garden on October 21 in private preview for select enterprise customers. When they open up, the same login will work for them too.

Every call lands on one Google Cloud bill, which makes it easier to compare models on cost and quality.

Step three: Give your app its own identity

Your app needs the same thing your developers just got: an identity instead of a key. For a workload, that identity is a service account.

The good news is that the code from Step 2 doesn't change. On your laptop, ADC picks up your own login. On Cloud Run, GKE or Compute Engine, it picks up a short-lived token for the service account attached to the workload, refreshed automatically. So there is nothing in your codebase to leak. A token that escapes is short-lived, usually about an hour, and it only carries the permissions of one service account.

Create the service account and deploy with it:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud iam service-accounts create agent-runtime \\\r\n --display-name="Runtime identity for the app"\r\n\r\ngcloud run deploy my-agent \\\r\n --image=us-docker.pkg.dev/my-startup-prod/agents/api:v1 \\\r\n --service-account=agent-runtime@my-startup-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com \\\r\n --region=us-central1'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f771128da10>)])]>

Keep people and production apart. Developers work in my-startup-dev under their own logins, and the app runs in my-startup-prod under its service account. A mistake in one doesn't spend the other's budget.

Step four: Give each identity only what it needs

Removing keys solves the leak problem. The next question is what each identity is allowed to do. If a person or a service account holds the Editor or Owner role, a stolen login or token can still delete resources, change permissions or read data it never needed.

Calling models takes one role, roles/aiplatform.user. The grant looks the same for both kinds of identity.

For people, grant it to a Google group, not to individuals. Onboarding and offboarding then become a group membership change:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding my-startup-dev \\\r\n --member="group:ai-builders@my-startup.com" \\\r\n --role="roles/aiplatform.user"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f771128e650>)])]>

For the app, grant it to the service account:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding my-startup-prod \\\r\n --member="serviceAccount:agent-runtime@my-startup-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \\\r\n --role="roles/aiplatform.user"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f771128f9d0>)])]>

It takes about 30 seconds longer than granting Editor. If anything is compromised later, the attacker gets one narrow role instead of the whole project. When someone leaves, remove them from the group and their access ends everywhere at once.

In the Cloud Console, the Grant access dialog has a Help me choose roles button. You describe the task in plain English and Gemini suggests predefined roles. By default the suggestions cover common tasks, which usually means a service's broad Admin, Editor or Viewer role. To get the narrow roles, say so:

What is the narrowest access a service account needs to call Gemini models on Agent Platform?

Three more controls are worth knowing:

  • If your project sits in an organization, the vertexai.allowedModels policy limits which models anyone can call. You list values such as publishers/google/models/gemini-4-hydrogen:predict, and everything else is blocked.

  • The repo includes a one-line audit that lists every service account holding Owner or Editor on a project. Run it now and again before each launch.

  • To stop new keys from being created, enforce Org Policies denying CREATE on apikeys.googleapis.com/Key for API keys and iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation for service account keys.

Step 5: Put the remaining keys in Secret Manager

Some keys won't go away, like Stripe, Slack or your email provider. They belong in Secret Manager, not in .env files, chat threads or the repo. Access works the way it did in Step 4: grant read access on each secret to the identity that needs it.

Test keys go to the developer group:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud secrets create stripe-test-key --data-file=-\r\ngcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding stripe-test-key \\\r\n --member="group:ai-builders@my-startup.com" \\\r\n --role="roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f771128cd10>)])]>

Anyone in the group can then fetch the key with their own login:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret=stripe-test-key'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f771128ff10>)])]>

Live keys stay in the production project, readable only by the app's service account. The app reads them at startup:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'from google.cloud import secretmanager\r\n\r\nsm = secretmanager.SecretManagerServiceClient()\r\nresp = sm.access_secret_version(\r\n name="projects/my-startup-prod/secrets/stripe-live-key/versions/latest"\r\n)\r\nstripe_key = resp.payload.data.decode("utf-8")'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f771128e110>)])]>

Reading --data-file=- from standard input keeps the value out of your shell history. Every read is tied to a named person or service account, and rotating a key means adding one new version. Nothing is redeployed and no file is copied between laptops.

Then finish the job. Go to the AI Studio API keys page and delete every key, personal or shared, that ever left a laptop. A key you have moved away from is still live until you delete it.

What the new setup gives you

Once your people and your app run on identities in a Google Cloud project, several protections become available that a bare key can't offer. You don't need all of them on day one. They are worth knowing about before your first launch.

A spend cap that pauses the service

Standard budget alerts send email while the bill keeps climbing. A spend cap budget, currently in Preview, does more. When estimated spend for one service in one project passes the amount you set, new requests to that service are paused until you lift the cap or the next month starts. Alerts go to billing admins and project owners at 50%, 80% and 100%.

You can create one in the console under Budgets & alerts by choosing Spend cap enforcement, or through the Budget API. The repo wraps the API call and has a dry-run flag so you can inspect the request first:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'python -m bonus_spend_cap.create_spend_cap \\\r\n --billing-account 012345-6789AB-CDEF01 --amount 500 --dry-run'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f771128d8d0>)])]>

Know the limits before relying on it. Each cap covers a single project and a single service. Agent Platform, the Gemini API, Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions are eligible today. Enforcement runs on estimated cost and is not instant. Any overage is billed as normal, so set the number below the amount you can actually afford to lose. A cap also pauses usage covered by commitments, and after you lift it the service can take up to an hour to recover.

Set one cap on the dev project and another on prod. An experiment then can't drain the budget your customers depend on. For a second layer, lower your Agent Platform quotas to what you really need, so a bug or an agent stuck in a loop runs into a ceiling instead of your card limit.

Guardrails on prompts and responses

As soon as real users can type into your app, someone will try to make it ignore its instructions. Model Armor screens prompts and responses for prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, malicious URLs and sensitive data. You create a template once, check each prompt against it and only call the model when it comes back clean. The repo has both halves.

A sandbox for model-written code

If your product lets the model write and run code, for example to analyze a customer's spreadsheet, that code should not run inside your application process. With code execution, the model runs Python in a Google-managed sandbox and hands back the result:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'config=types.GenerateContentConfig(\r\n tools=[types.Tool(code_execution=types.ToolCodeExecution())],\r\n)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f771128dc90>)])]>

The generated code never sees your environment variables, your files or your database.

Someone watching for unusual behavior

Security Command Center surfaces threats and misconfigurations across the project, such as a service account suddenly calling an API it has never used or a workload contacting an unfamiliar host. Together with Cloud Audit Logs, which record who changed what and when, it also gives you the answers your first enterprise customer's security review will ask for. Because every call now comes from a named person or service account, those logs mean something.

Your 20-minute checklist

For your team:

  • Everyone runs gcloud auth application-default login.

  • Grant roles/aiplatform.user to one Google group, and enable the partner models you want.

  • Move shared test keys into Secret Manager, readable by the group.

For your app:

  • Deploy with a service account that holds roles/aiplatform.user and nothing broader.

  • Move live third-party keys into Secret Manager, readable only by that service account.

  • Set a spend cap on each project below the amount you can afford to lose.

For both: Run the key scanner, then delete every AI Studio key at aistudio.google.com/apikey.

None of this slows down building. You keep the speed of the prototype and every model in Model Garden stays one string away. Nobody on the team has to guard a key again. The full code, with a sample for every step and bonus above, is in the companion repo.

items.title: Evaluating safeguarding in multi-turn conversations with AI assistants
items.summary: Conversational AI assistants are now used for personal and emotional support. Developers report improvements in how new models respond to sensitive conversations, yet users and civil society continue to raise concerns about their behaviour in real-world, repeated interactions that safety evaluations rarely capture. Often, evaluations present signs of distress clearly and in a single message, even though people may reveal their struggles gradually in otherwise ordinary conversations. We worked with three community mental health support workers to test if models provide the same level of safeguarding when cues are shared all at once or gradually over time. We designed nine scenarios in which a user shares cues related to depression, psychosis, or domestic abuse. For each scenario, the support workers established a gold standard response, ranging from signposting support to pausing the everyday task to address safeguarding. We presented five cues either together in one message or dispersed across a conversation. Across more than 7,400 conversations, we evaluated six widely used models from five developers. GPT-5.5, Grok 4.3, DeepSeek V4, and Llama 4 Maverick met the support workers' standards in just 26-59% of conversations when cues were concentrated, and only 3-6% when dispersed. Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5 showed a smaller gap, meeting the standards in 68-97% of concentrated conversations and 59-87% of dispersed conversations. Even the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5, fell short of the gold standard in 13% of conversations when cues were dispersed. Safety evaluations centred on explicit, legible concerns can overstate how well safeguards protect people when signs of distress emerge gradually or indirectly through ordinary conversations. For claims of improved safety to be taken seriously, developers must design and assess safeguards around how people actually communicate.

items.title: Harnessing Medical Visual-Language Models with Agentic Evidence Management
items.summary: Medical vision-language agents increasingly rely on segmentation tools, and recent work has focused on acquiring the right mask, often treating a good mask as the end point of tool use. But do these agents use the resulting evidence effectively? To answer this question, we need a benchmark that separates evidence use from segmentation quality, spans multiple medical image types, and allows the same mask to be presented in different ways. Existing medical VQA datasets do not jointly provide these properties. We therefore construct Mask-Evidence MedVQA, a 2.5K-example benchmark spanning four image types, where each question is paired with an answer-relevant ground-truth mask and multiple possible renderings. Our study reveals two limitations of direct tool use. First, evidence presentation matters. Different renderings of the same fixed mask can substantially change model behavior. Second, masks introduce an evidence trade-off. Highlighting a relevant region can expose diagnostic evidence the model previously missed, but the added visual cue can also induce incorrect associations. As a result, even a ground-truth mask can correct some answers while turning initially correct ones into incorrect ones. Together, these findings show that acquiring the right mask is not enough. An agent must also decide how to present the evidence and whether it should change the answer. We therefore introduce TUNE (Tool Use is Not Enough), an evidence-management harness that explicitly manages what evidence to acquire, how to present it, and whether to accept the resulting answer update. Across three public medical VQA benchmarks, evidence management improves the fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B backbone's mean accuracy by 4.0 percentage points. Full TUNE improves over direct tool use by 9.1 points on average across seven benchmarks and achieves competitive results against existing medical VLMs and agents.

items.title: Complete-SVD: A Functional Norm Approach to Low-Rank LLM Compression
items.summary: Post-training low-rank compression of neural networks must not only approximate the original weights but also preserve the model's input-output behavior. Recent output-aware methods measure the compression error beyond the compressed layer, at the model output, weighting logit changes by the observed next token or by the model's predicted probabilities. We propose Complete-SVD, a method for large language models that minimizes the $L_2$ distance between the logits of the original and compressed models, weighting all logit changes equally. Linearizing the network around the original weights, together with a Kronecker-factored approximation, reduces this objective to a weighted SVD with a closed-form solution. Its output-side factor is intractable to compute; we estimate it without bias from random probes, at a cost of $K$ backward passes per sequence, independent of vocabulary size and sequence length. At matched settings with uniform ranks and WikiText-2 calibration, Complete-SVD achieves the lowest C4 and PTB perplexity in every setting, and at ratio 0.7 under LEMS rank allocation. Replacing the $L_2$ distance by the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL-SVD), with the same estimation framework, lowers calibration perplexity in most settings and raises downstream accuracy, but raises cross-corpus perplexity. Complete-SVD also improves IFEval instruction-following accuracy over the strongest prior output-aware methods throughout.

  • Improved startup time on Windows when PATH points to Git for Windows' bin folder, by starting git.exe directly instead of through its launcher
  • Windows: Improved PowerShell tool speed by up to about half a second per command
  • Improved how soon the Bash tool's diff of changed files is ready in auto and bypass permissions modes
  • Improved speed of the Bash permission check on very deeply nested missing paths on macOS and Linux, and of secret masking on very long text with a URL
  • Improved transcript search to find text in edits and written files
  • Improved speed of reading large PNG images, and the quality of the JPEG sent in their place
  • Improved the Artifact tool to read an uploaded file by the address the artifact's page shows; other forms still fail, most with a message that says to read uploads one per call, by id
  • Improved the Artifact tool to ignore prompt, limit and label on some calls that do not use them instead of failing the call
  • Improved MCP server pages in /mcp: local, remote and agent servers share one layout, menus end in Back, and actions are no longer numbered outside screen reader mode; use the arrow keys and Enter
  • Improved narrow terminals: /status, forms and detail screens lay out better, /model and /effort fit at about 40 columns, and key hints such as ←/→ to adjust stay
  • Improved /install-github-app: the repository, secret and API key steps use the standard list and keys, with shorter messages, a spinner and clearer errors
  • Improved /desktop: the download question is a standard list instead of y/n
  • Changed ExitWorktree to ask before removing a worktree that may hold unsaved work; refused in don't-ask mode or with nobody to answer, unless an allow rule, auto or bypass permissions mode allows it
  • Changed claude mcp add --scope project to stop, instead of overwriting the file, when .mcp.json lists its servers at the top level with no mcpServers key
  • Changed the arrow keys on most permission prompts to stop at No instead of wrapping around; a number past the last answer moves to No
  • Changed path checks to refuse some symbolic links
  • Changed what counts as inside a working directory, so some paths now ask for permission
  • Changed permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories to ask about more Bash commands in bypass and auto modes, and to deny some in auto mode
  • Changed permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories to refuse more Bash commands that name a path under a Read or Edit deny rule, where it used to ask
  • Changed auto mode's notice about falling back to billed classifier requests to say that an upcoming release removes the fallback; each action it would have checked will be asked about or denied
  • Changed auto mode to ignore more allow rules that run any package, like Bash(pnpm dlx *), and path or version forms of ones it already ignored (/usr/bin/npm run:*); the safety check decides those
  • Changed /sandbox and most /config value lists to be unnumbered outside screen reader mode; use the arrow keys and Enter
  • Changed Bash commands whose variables expand to very long text to be denied, with a message that says to use shorter values or a file
  • Changed the PowerShell tool to ask before one more command, even under a rule naming it; if nothing answers, it's refused unless a whole-tool rule, auto mode or bypass permissions mode allows it
  • Changed a subagent resumed by a sibling's message to follow the session's permission settings; it may now ask, or be refused where nobody can answer
  • Changed --worktree with a relative --add-dir beside the launch folder to give the Bash sandbox that folder, not one beside the worktree
  • Changed some --worktree starts with a relative --add-dir above the launch folder, such as .., to give the Bash sandbox, and a --bg session, only the worktree
  • Changed Claude in Chrome to refuse uploading some credential files; attach those to the page yourself
  • Changed artifact approval in organizations that require it for each new artifact: an artifact that only a plugin created or allowed can be refused
  • Changed sessions with nobody to ask to refuse a new artifact at once, with no permission prompt, in organizations that require approval of each one
  • Changed the Artifact tool to refuse calls once settings turn Artifacts off, in sessions already running too
  • Changed the Artifact publish prompt to stop offering "don't ask again" in subagents and after a background task result, someone else's message or a compaction
  • Changed claude plugin eval to keep its deny rules over a plugin's permission hook, and to flag calls the hook let through
  • Changed MCP server logs to record the mode, action, and field names of elicitation requests and hook answers, not their full contents
  • Changed most prompts to ignore answers other than Esc for a moment after resuming with fg
  • Changed Code Mode to no longer refuse to start when an installed mod hooks tool calls; an administrator can still keep Code Mode off in managed settings
  • Changed subagents launched without a model to stay on the model they started on when resumed, including after /model
  • Changed the first subagent on a model to wait up to 1.5 seconds (10 in claude -p) for that model's settings from Anthropic, instead of starting without them
  • Changed restarted background subagents, and turns that start by themselves, to wait for plugins to load
  • Changed prompt history to leave out most launch prompts of sessions that another Claude Code session started, such as claude --bg run by Claude
  • Changed subagent progress summaries in terminal sessions on Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI and Microsoft Foundry to be written from short notes, not the whole conversation, using far fewer tokens

items.title: Release 2.75.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.11
items.summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • PyTorch backend: Added AOTI BF16 input/output support.
  • THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt is now included in the containers.
  • Fixed a use-after-free in the dynamic batcher and a preserve_ordering completion-slot issue on response-cache hits.
  • Prevented silent gRPC stream cancellations under backpressure.
  • Bounded the decompressed HTTP inference response size in the client library.
  • Perf Analyzer: Honored supplied output shapes, propagated the binary exit code, tagged the wheel as platform-specific, and limited profile-data export to the needed inputs and outputs.
  • Python backend: Now logs when the backend stub exits on a crash signal.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
